name: Dimensionally Continued Black Holes
description: The static, spherically symmetric black holes of Lovelock's theory of gravity with every coefficient set by one length, which Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Jorge Zanelli found in 1994. In odd dimensions the action is a Chern-Simons form and a gap of naked singularities separates anti-de Sitter space from the black holes, as in three dimensions; in even dimensions the black holes are continuations of Schwarzschild's in anti-de Sitter space.
convention: The length $\ell$ fixes every coefficient of Lovelock's action, and the mass $M$ is a pure number in odd dimensions and a length in even ones [banados1994]. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Every two dimensions added to spacetime give David Lovelock's theory of gravity one more constant [banados1994, ilha1997]. Lovelock found in 1971 the most general field equations of second order for the metric [lovelock1971, banados1994]. In $D$ dimensions the action is a sum over the even dimensions below $D$, each contributing its Euler density continued to $D$ with its own coefficient, and Claudio Teitelboim and Jorge Zanelli built its Hamiltonian in 1987 [teitelboim1987]. With the coefficients left free, the metric components of a static, spherically symmetric solution are roots of a polynomial of degree $n - 1$ "which cannot be solved explicitly", in the words of Máximo Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli, where $D = 2n$ in even dimensions and $D = 2n - 1$ in odd ones [banados1994]. Such a theory has up to $n - 1$ of these solutions, each may have a horizon for either sign of the energy, and the entropy of its black holes can decrease as the horizon grows [banados1994].¶Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli tied every coefficient to one length $\ell$ in 1994, leaving Newton's constant and a negative cosmological constant proportional to $-1/\ell^2$ [banados1994]. They enlarged the Lorentz group to the anti-de Sitter group $SO(D-1,2)$, and in odd dimensions their Lagrangian is the Chern-Simons form of that group, whose exterior derivative is the Euler density of $D + 1$ dimensions [banados1994]. Ali Chamseddine had built gravity in five dimensions on a Chern-Simons form in 1989, and in every odd dimension the year after [chamseddine1989, chamseddine1990]. In even dimensions no nontrivial action is invariant under the whole group, so they kept the Lorentz group, with a Lagrangian they called "the gravitational analogue of the Born-Infeld Lagrangian" [banados1994]. In three dimensions the Chern-Simons action, and in four the Born-Infeld one, is Einstein's with a negative cosmological constant [banados1994]. The field equations are a product of $n - 1$ factors of the anti-de Sitter curvature, so anti-de Sitter space of radius $\ell$ solves them in every dimension [banados1994].¶For a static, spherically symmetric field they found the metric function $$f(r) = 1 - \left(\frac{2M}{r}\right)^{1/(n-1)} + \frac{r^2}{\ell^2}$$ in even dimensions and $$f(r) = 1 - (M + 1)^{1/(n-1)} + \frac{r^2}{\ell^2}$$ in odd ones, with the mass $M$ a length in the first and a pure number in the second, in their units [banados1994]. At $n = 2$ the first is Schwarzschild's black hole in anti-de Sitter space, and the second is the black hole of three dimensions without rotation, called BTZ after the three, who had found it in 1992 [banados1994, banados1992]. Cecilia Garraffo and Gaston Giribet wrote in 2008 that the three "discovered the BTZ as a particular case of a family of Lovelock black holes they were studying at that time" [garraffo2008]. For odd $n$ the root has two signs, and with the negative one a positive mass has a naked singularity; the three ruled that out as "a form of cosmic censorship" and set aside the dimensions of odd $n$, beginning with five and six [banados1994]. Javier P. Muniain and Dardo Píriz kept those dimensions in 1996 by taking the positive root, which has a regular horizon [muniain1996]. In odd dimensions the black holes have $M \ge 0$, anti-de Sitter space is the solution with $M = -1$, and the two are separated "by a gap of naked curvature singularities", as in three dimensions [banados1994].¶Above three dimensions the curvature varies with $r$ and is singular at $r = 0$, and no identification of points in anti-de Sitter space produces these black holes [banados1994]. Their temperature is $$T = \frac{\hbar c}{4\pi k_B}\,\frac{1 + (2n-1)\,r_+^2/\ell^2}{(n-1)\,r_+}$$ in even dimensions and $T = \hbar c\,r_+/(2\pi k_B\ell^2)$ in odd ones, with $r_+$ the horizon radius [banados1994]. A black hole of even dimension grows hotter without limit as it shrinks, and one of odd dimension cools toward zero [banados1994]. The three obtained the entropy as a surface term of the action at the horizon, and found that it grows with $r_+$ and differs from a quarter of the area above four dimensions [banados1994]. Ted Jacobson and Robert Myers had found in 1993 that the entropy of a stationary black hole in Lovelock's theory is a quarter of the area plus "a sum of intrinsic curvature invariants integrated over a cross section of the horizon", and the three found their own in agreement [jacobson1993, banados1994]. In a letter of 1994 the three derived the entropy from the Gauss-Bonnet theorem continued to higher dimension, and found the factor in front of the area in Einstein's theory to be the Euler class of a small disk at the horizon [banados1994entropy].¶Muniain and Píriz found that the heat capacity of a black hole of even dimension changes sign at $r_+ = \ell/\sqrt{D-1}$, where its temperature is lowest, and that one of odd dimension has no such transition [muniain1996]. Rong-Gen Cai and Kwang-Sup Soh replaced the sphere of the horizon with a flat or a hyperbolic space in 1999, and found the heat capacity positive at every radius [cai1999]. Juan Crisóstomo, Ricardo Troncoso, and Zanelli set both families in 2000 at the end of a list of theories with one anti-de Sitter vacuum, numbered by the highest power $k$ of the curvature, with Einstein's theory at $k = 1$ [crisostomo2000]. Of the black holes on that list, they found, only the Chern-Simons ones come to equilibrium with a heat bath at any temperature [crisostomo2000]. Xiao-Mei Kuang and Olivera Miskovic found in 2017 that the charged black holes of even dimension with a spherical horizon pass through a transition like that of a van der Waals fluid, and those of odd dimension through none [kuang2017].¶Anderson Ilha and José Lemos joined a collapsing ball of dust to these black holes in even dimensions in 1997 and found that a horizon forms, and with Antares Kleber did the same in odd dimensions in 1999 [ilha1997, ilha1999]. Masato Nozawa and Hideki Maeda made the mass a function of advanced time in 2006, for null dust falling into anti-de Sitter space, and found that a naked singularity can form, null in even dimensions and timelike in odd ones [nozawa2006]. Luis Avilés, José Díaz, Cristian Quinzacara, and Patricio Salgado followed a cloud of dust of uneven density in five dimensions in a preprint of 2026, and found an apparent horizon only around shells whose enclosed mass exceeds a threshold [aviles2026]. Kiyoshi Shiraishi and Takuya Maki derived the propagator of a conformal scalar field on the black holes of odd dimension in 1994, and computed the vacuum expectation value of its square in five dimensions [shiraishi1994]. Chern-Simons gravity in three dimensions has no local degrees of freedom, and Bañados, Luis Garay, and Marc Henneaux showed in 1996 that its counterparts in higher odd dimensions have them [banados1996].

related.text: The even family at $n = 2$, in four dimensions, where the metric function is $1 - 2M/r + r^2/\ell^2$ and the theory is Einstein's [banados1994].

The odd family in three dimensions is this black hole without rotation. There the curvature is constant and the black hole is anti-de Sitter space with points identified, and from five dimensions up the curvature varies with $r$ [banados1994].
The solution with $M = -1$ in odd dimensions and with $M = 0$ in even ones. In odd dimensions naked singularities fill the masses between it and the black holes [banados1994].

The black hole of five dimensions with the Gauss-Bonnet coupling left free. With a negative cosmological constant tuned to that coupling the two vacua of the theory merge into one anti-de Sitter space, and its black hole is the dimensionally continued one of five dimensions [nozawa2006, aviles2026].

Black holes of anti-de Sitter space with flat and hyperbolic horizons, in Einstein's theory. Rong-Gen Cai and Kwang-Sup Soh gave the dimensionally continued black holes the same horizons in 1999 [cai1999].

The black hole of Einstein's theory in $D$ dimensions with no cosmological constant, whose metric function falls as $1/r^{D-3}$. In even dimensions the dimensionally continued one without a cosmological constant is $1 - (2M/r)^{1/(n-1)}$, with its horizon at $r = 2M$ [banados1994].

A ball of dust collapsing to Schwarzschild's black hole. Anderson Ilha, Antares Kleber, and José Lemos joined the same ball to these black holes, in even dimensions in 1997 and in odd ones in 1999 [ilha1997, ilha1999].

A black hole fed by null dust, its mass a function of advanced time. Masato Nozawa and Hideki Maeda let the mass of these black holes depend on advanced time in 2006 and found that a naked singularity can form [nozawa2006].

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Mass, a pure number in five dimensions, with $M \ge 0$ for a black hole and $M = -1$ for anti-de Sitter space
The length that fixes every coefficient of the action, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space at $M = -1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with $t$ a time and $\psi$, $\theta$, $\phi$ the angles of the 3-sphere. The metric function is $1 - \sqrt{M + 1} + r^2/\ell^2$ with the positive square root [banados1994, muniain1996], and it vanishes on the horizon $r_+ = \ell\sqrt{\sqrt{M + 1} - 1}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Mass, a pure number in five dimensions, with $M \ge 0$ for a black hole and $M = -1$ for anti-de Sitter space
The length that fixes every coefficient of the action, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space at $M = -1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - \sqrt{M + 1} + r^2/\ell^2\right)^{-1}$ with the positive square root [nozawa2006].

coordinates.name: Conformal, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Mass, a pure number in five dimensions, with $M \ge 0$ for a black hole and $M = -1$ for anti-de Sitter space
The length that fixes every coefficient of the action, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space at $M = -1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with $t$ a time, outside the horizon $r_+ = \ell\sqrt{\sqrt{M + 1} - 1}$ of a black hole with $M > 0$, the square root taken positive. The areal radius is $r = r_+\sec\rho$, and the conformal factor is $\ell^2\sec^2\rho$ [shiraishi1994]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical, Six Dimensions

parameters.description: Mass, a length in six dimensions, with $M > 0$ for a black hole and $M = 0$ for anti-de Sitter space
The length that fixes every coefficient of the action, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space at $M = 0$
The root in the metric function, a pure number

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \chi, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 6$, with $t$ a time and $\chi$, $\psi$, $\theta$, $\phi$ the angles of the 4-sphere. The metric function is $1 - w + r^2/\ell^2$ with $w = \sqrt{2M/r}$ the positive square root [banados1994, muniain1996], and it vanishes on the horizon $r_+$, where $r_+\left(1 + r_+^2/\ell^2\right)^2 = 2M$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(\ell^2\,w + 4r^2\right)\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)}{4\ell^4\,r}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{\ell^2\,w + 4r^2}{4r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)}{\ell^2}\dot{\chi}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi}{\ell^2}\dot{\psi}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi\sin^2\psi}{\ell^2}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi\sin^2\psi\sin^2\theta}{\ell^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

parameters.description: Mass, a length in six dimensions, with $M > 0$ for a black hole and $M = 0$ for anti-de Sitter space
The length that fixes every coefficient of the action, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space at $M = 0$
The root in the metric function, a pure number

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \chi, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 6$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - w + r^2/\ell^2\right)^{-1}$ with $w = \sqrt{2M/r}$ the positive square root [nozawa2006]. The horizon $r_+$ is the root of $r_+\left(1 + r_+^2/\ell^2\right)^2 = 2M$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(\ell^2\,w + 4r^2\right)\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)}{4\ell^4\,r}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{\ell^2\,w + 4r^2}{2\ell^2\,r}\dot{v}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)}{\ell^2}\dot{\chi}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi}{\ell^2}\dot{\psi}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi\sin^2\psi}{\ell^2}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\ell^2\left(1 - w\right) + r^2\right)\sin^2\chi\sin^2\psi\sin^2\theta}{\ell^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
